newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba officials say no shortcuts to adopt the Euro.
newsitem.headline: Buba officials say no shortcuts to adopt the Euro.

text.p: Stepping up a public relations campaign for Europe's currency union as its 1999 starting date nears, two Bundesbank officials warned on Monday there would be no shortcuts into the union, if the Euro currency is to succeed.

Both echoed Germany's uncompromising demand that nations must meet a slew of entry criteria to join economic and monetary union (EMU), but one of them argued that the Maastricht Treaty left room for the interpretion of those criteria.

"The treaty for the currency union only forbids excessive deficits," Welteke said, urging Europeans not to become bogged down with emotional public debate about the exact figures countries need to meet the criteria.

"But the reference values, that a public deficit should not exceed three percent of gross domestic product and that government debt must not exceed 60 percent of gross domestic product, are already enshrined in the treaty on Europe's economic union," Welteke told businesmen and women.

"We want to achieve sustainable fiscal austerity and that doesn't necessarily need to be 63 percent," Welteke, who is also president of the central bank in the regional state of Hesse said, adding: "In some cases, having a budget deficit of three percent to gross domestic product is far too much."
But seeking ward off fears Germany was ready to let everyone into EMU, Welteke stressed that the Bundesbank would not give up its insistence on strict adherence to the criteria.
"I am only arguing that the fiscal criteria be interpreted as they are laid down in the treaty. And these criteria should not be overinterpreted," Welteke said in reply to questions.
"No nation should be allowed in (to EMU) which does not show a sufficient amount of stability," Welteke said.

In Berlin, Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, who is also president of the central bank in city-state Berlin and in Brandenburg state, told a meeting of bankers he opposed any softening of entry criteria.

"If there is any horse trading, then it can be feared that people will shift into other currencies. This could result in great turbulence and nations might exit from the common currency," Kuehbacher said.

Welteke was echoing remarks Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer made several days ago. By pointing out that the treaty allows for some leeway he neither contradicted Kuehbacher nor hinted at a rift between Bundesbank council members.
In meeting the two fiscal criteria, nations must present stable exchange rates, low inflation rates and moderate interest rates in order to be admitted to the currency union.
Their 1997 economic data will be evaluated by a group of politicians in 1998 who will then determine which nations will actually be allowed to join on January 1, 1999.
Welteke said Germany and France would be among the first group to join "as a currency union without them would make no political sense".
He said a further five or six nations should be in ready to participate in EMU by that time, bringing the total number of participants to seven or eight.

"You can figure out which nations are likely to among those participating," Welteke said. He refused to comment on speculation over whether Italy, which at the weekend scrambled back into the ERM as part of a bid to be among the first group to join EMU, would actually make it.

Welteke shrugged off calls for the currency union to be delayed, saying that savings packages, put together now as part of efforts to join the currency union, would need to be implemented in any case.
"We need the spending cuts anyway, they cannot be blamed on the European currency union," he said.
